speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to discuss an important and urgent matter.
As the April, 1976 dairy policy of the Minister of Agriculture led to an income loss of roughly 20 per cent for milk producers and the lay-off of many farm labourers; as agricultural producers must now bear the attacks, wrong-doings and iniquities of the Department of National Revenue and the Unemployment Insurance Commission; as civil servants would seem to have decided to do away with that agricultural sector by refusing to insure that type of work, which could lead to its complete disappearance while depriving it of the assistance required for its development, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That this House order the Minister of National Revenue and the head of the Unemployment Insurance Commission respectively to take all necessary steps, as soon as possible, to remedy the many weaknesses that exist with regard to unemployment insurance in the case of farm labourers.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that since the present administration took power in 1968, unemployment levels in Quebec have been approximately one third higher than the national rate while in the Atlantic provinces the unemployment level has been 50 per cent higher than the national average, and since, to judge from an answer to a question put to him yesterday the Minister of Finance is apparently unaware of these facts, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander):
That there be an immediate reference of the question of the level and nature of unemployment in Canada, particularly in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces, to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs which has been sitting idle and not reviewing economic matters for months.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with a matter of pressing necessity.
Since tension is constantly increasing in Quebec penitentiaries, especially at Saint-Vincent-de-Paul and at the CDC, and since that condition has reached its climax and we can no longer tolerate the fact that prisoners are kept in their cells 2V/2 hours out of 24,1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday):
That this House unanimously recommend to the Solicitor General: first, the construction in the shortest possible time of a penitentiary in Quebec to prevent crowding of inmates in existing penitentiaries; second, the establishment in that new institution of an adequate rehabilitation program; third, the use of available premises in existing penitentiaries for preliminary rehabilitation programs; and finally, the setting up of a mechanism enabling inmates to receive visitors.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Does the right hon. gentleman believe that the action he took in 1973, almost four years ago, when this matter was first brought to his attention, was at all adequate? speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Yesterday the Prime Minister referred with a sense of self-satisfaction to the billion dollars transferred disproportionately to upper-income Canadians as a result of the indexation of our tax system. He suggested this would be an added stimulus to the economy to create jobs. Since this billion dollars relates precisely to a change in the cost of living and was designed to do so, would the Prime Minister now admit his error and acknowledge that there is no new stimulus to the economy in this at all, precisely because there is no change in purchasing power. If he makes such a rare acknowledgement of error, would he agree that such stimulus is now required?

subsubtopic: RESEARCH ON THE EFFECTS OF CARBON BLACK ON HUMAN HEALTH
speechtext: What research projects is the Department of National Health and Welfare sponsoring or conducting on the effects of Carbon Black (food grade) on human health?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: RESEARCH ON THE EFFECTS OF CARBON BLACK ON HUMAN HEALTH
speechtext: At present, the Department of National Health and Welfare has underway studies to1 assess the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) content of samples of food grade carbon black presently used in Canada. Results of this study are not yet available. Recently, the U.S. has placed restrictions on the most common methods of producing food grade carbon black. There is evidence in the literature to suggest that the carbon black may actually protect experimental animals from the effects of PAH impurities. The Department of National Health and Welfare, in addition to conducting studies, is continuously surveying world literature on carbon black.

subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: STUDIES ON CO-CARCINOGENS IN CANADIAN FOOD SUPPLY
speechtext: What research projects is the Department of National Health and Welfare sponsoring or conducting on the possible existence of co-carcinogens in the Canadian food supply?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: STUDIES ON CO-CARCINOGENS IN CANADIAN FOOD SUPPLY
speechtext:
The Department of National Health and Welfare has ongoing research programs to identify co-carcinogens in the food supply. These programs involve testing of food additives, environmental contaminants, pesticides and natural toxins, for potential mutagenic (carcinogenic) effects both singly and in combination with known carcinogens or mutagens. Analytical methods are being used in an attempt to identify suspect co-carcinogens in foods and food additives. These research programs also involve extensive review and evaluation of world literature on co-carcinogenesis on a contin-
[Mr. Cullen.)
uous basis. This includes maintaining liaison with experts in the WHO and FAO, U.S. National Cancer Institute and the International Agency for Research on Cancer in Lyon, France. Scientists of the Department serve as advisors and consultants to these groups with respect to carcinogenesis in general.

subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: RESEARCH ON COMBINATORY EFFECTS OF ADDITIVES IN THE CANADIAN FOOD SUPPLY
speechtext: What research projects is the Department of National Health and Welfare sponsoring or conducting on the combinatory effects of additives in the Canadian food supply?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: RESEARCH ON COMBINATORY EFFECTS OF ADDITIVES IN THE CANADIAN FOOD SUPPLY
speechtext: The Department of National Health and Welfare does not have a research program specifically on the combinatory effects of food additives in the Canadian food supply. To be effective, such a program would require massive concentration of resources and is feasible only on an international scale. Attempts are being made by Canada and other countries, to initiate international collaboration on such research. However, the department tests many food additive combinations as part of the research programs on co-carcinogens in the food supply (See Parliamentary Inquiry No. 1126). In addition, departmental scientists continuously monitor world literature to obtain all available information on the combinatory effects of food additives.

speechtext: Changes in human moods or emotions may be associated with allergenicity and/or hyperkinesis and behavioral problems. The Department of National Health and Welfare, in conjunction with an outside agency through a health grant, is sponsoring a research program to identify food constituents which may be responsible for the induction of hyperkinetic states or learning difficulties in children. Children are being tested for allergies to certain food components, and will be tested for allergies to food additives when adequate analytical methods are available. Such methods are currently being developed by departmental scientists. The Department is fully aware of world research on the possible relationship between food additives and mood changes, including mood changes associated with hyperactivity. The matter of artificial food additives and the effects they may have on human moods and emotions has previously been discussed in the House of Commons during private member's hour, October 29, 1976. speechtext:
That in relation to Bill C-22, an act to amend the statute law relating to income tax, one sitting day shall be allotted to the further consideration and third reading and passage stage of the bill; that at the end of the said sitting day any proceedings before the House shall be interrupted if required for the purpose of this order, and any question then necessary in order to dispose of the third reading and passage stage of the bill shall be put forthwith and successively without further debate or amendment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-22 and the budget proposals which that bill contains have been before the House since May 25, and in addition to the nine sitting days on which the bill has been under debate in the House during the current session the proposals which the bill embodies were the subject matter of six days' debate during the course of consideration of the budget last spring. In the circumstances, I think one can fairly say that this period of time, including the day involved in the order now before the House, will amount to a full two weeks of House sittings and that this is more than ample time for the House to consider and debate these proposals.
It has, however, ceased to be a question of debate at this point. The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) has indicated an intention to take all the future time of the House in debating this particular matter: I would refer hon. members to his speech in the course of the debate on Monday last. I would like to return more especially to the application of S.O. 75C. We all know that there are two other means to achieve the same result. At present, we have S.O. 75A and 75B. In S.O. 75A, when there is agreement among all parties, the government House leader rises and may propose a motion which is passed without debate and it is also a matter of time allotment, but merely as a result of an agreement between parties.
In S.O. 75B, the government is allowed to do the same when a majority of parties feel that the time has come to set a limit for those proceedings although a party or a group of members may disagree. Perhaps I might take a couple of minutes to deal with the substance of the closure motion. Let me say at the outset that I agree with the government's right to impose closure. I agree that a government which has a majority in the House of Commons-whether or not it represents the majority of the voters-must have the right to exercise and implement the collective will of the government after a reasonable amount of time in debate has elapsed. So, unlike some members of the House who argue that closure is inappropriate in principle, I do not take that view; I think it is appropriate.
The question, then, is: At what point is it justified? I think it is extraordinarily important in this debate to remember that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) first spoke to closure, which he applied after only 4'/2 days of debate on a finance measure which goes to the root of the justification of parliamentary democracy in the first place-because parliaments were first formed to justify spending by the monarch- the minister did not even attempt to justify closure. Nowhere in his speech did he allude to the need for invoking closure on parliament, for cutting off discussion of this important matter after only 4'/2 days. He spoke only to the finance measures that we were considering. Not once did he offer any argument to justify closure.
Liberal members have again spoken in the House today, but there has been no justification put forward for bringing in closure on a finance measure after very limited debate. The

I would say to the hon. member that that is only ritualisti-cally true, that all citizens are open to benefits. This is like saying, as was said in the eighteenth century in opposition to the French aristocracy, that rich man and poor man alike have the right to sleep on a bridge over the Seine. But is it only coincidence that the poor have this experience? The point is that every one of the provisions that are open to the rich and the poor in this bill are overwhelmingly used by the rich because they provide overwhelming tax benefits for the rich. When they save on their taxes, it has to be made up by other taxpayers in this country.
If you want to extend pension benefits to the people of Canada, you should not do it by providing a tax rip-off for the majority of those in the upper income brackets. You should extend the benefits that are provided under the Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act. They way to do it is to deal directly with the matter, not through some indirect tax benefit. Or if you are interested in improving day care, you do not do so by lifting disproportionately the tax burden on the rich. You do it by providing a direct grant, a demogrant, a cash payment with the same cash value for rich and poor alike, so that everyone can pay for day care. You do not give a tax benefit worth several hundred dollars to the rich and perhaps give nothing at all to a man or woman who is out working, has kids at home but is not in a position to pay any taxes at all. Mr. Speaker, I am trying to be very serious about this. It is quite obvious that the Liberals and the hecklers over there cannot be serious, and never have been. The discussions and debates in the House are based on freedom of speech, and we must preserve it. Whether you like it or not, a closure motion takes away that freedom. I do not agree with the filibuster, but I totally disagree with any attempt to take away one's right to speak.

We have many things to do in this country, and we cannot do them entirely under the adversary system. Every member of parliament has rights and obligations in the House, and we should have the freedom to protect those rights and obligations. Surely taxation by closure is not proper, and surely taxation without representation is not proper. I suggest that the effect of this closure motion, if it is passed, might be to take away a person's right to representation. If so, it would result in taxation without representation. The House is scheduled to sit 47 more days from now until April 6, which is the usual date for beginning the Easter adjournment. There are seven allotted days, which reduces the number of days available for government business to 40. If the work of this session is to be completed by a reasonable time this summer, we must operate in the way in which the people of Canada expect us to operate, in an effective and businesslike fashion.
What we have seen from hon. members opposite, particularly from members of the New Democratic Party in the present context, is an effort to try to bring this institution to a grinding halt. They may see some political advantage in that. It may be in relation to the present measure which is before the House, the Income Tax Act. However, I suspect it is broader than that, because they feel it might well be in their political interest to try to bring this institution to a halt, to make it inefficient, to obstruct it and to keep it from doing the business of the country so that they can then heap abuse or discredit on the government when they themselves are the authors and architects of that inefficiency and inability to do business.
I think the Minister of Finance deserves the credit of this House for taking the step he has taken to bring this debate to an end and to establish a measure of efficiency here so that we can do what we have been elected to do, and that is to consider the business of the country and to do so efficiently.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we were on the subject of Bill C-35 yesterday I was in the process of outlining the fact that while the bill may have the effect of correcting certain inequities in our pension system, it also has a very substantial amount of material missing, such as proposals which are
required in order to facilitate care of the elderly in this country. I was indicating that in my view the practice of the last two decades, which has been based largely on institutionalizing our elderly citizens, was probably not the right approach, besides being a little too costly. I was in the process of making a plea to the government, for as long as it has the responsibility of government, to take the action necessary to provide alternative services for elderly citizens.
I think we would all agree that institutions of various types which are dedicated to the care of the elderly are necessary for our senior citizens. But we also know that keeping the elderly at home in their own environment for as long as they wish is far more desirable than simply throwing them into an institution and forgetting about them until they are dead. However, the situation in Canada is such that services which are required to achieve this aim are very sadly lacking, and I wanted to conclude my comments by outlining some of the measures that need to be taken if, indeed, we are to create an environment which would allow our elderly citizens to remain in their own homes or in the homes of their families to the maximum extent possible.
First of all, there should be a larger number of the day hospital type of institution. It is suggested that patients would be admitted only in the day time. That would certainly help to decrease the number of admissions and facilitate earlier discharge. It is also suggested that an emergency care "flying squad" would be very useful. The experience of a hospital in England has shown the value of a geriatric flying squad which consists of a multi-disciplinary team comprising a physician, public health nurse and social worker, and can respond to emergency situations developing in the community by giving advice, or a visit being made by one of the team. This team would be based in the day hospital and would consist of day hospital personnel responding to telephone requests for assistance from patients on the day hospital roster.
There is also need for a large number of geriatric consultation clinics. It would be useful to increase the number of these clinics to provide for increased referrals from family practitioners and health centres. There is also need for early diagnostic health examinations to be carried out on a greater scale and to be more readily available. Here, assessments of the elderly would provide early diagnosis of treatable conditions, with the assessment of social circumstances aimed at improving the home environment and utilizing community resources, working in close liais.on with other departments such as departments of ophthalmology and otolaryngology, podiatry and orthopedics.
There is also a need for follow-up clinics. An enlargement of these services would be necessary for the continuing care of elderly patients who have been discharged and do not have their own family practitioner. This would have obvious possibilities in regard to education for undergraduates, resident physicians and other health professionals. It would also increase opportunities for research projects in the area of geriatrics.

February 9, 1977

Finally, Mr. Speaker, there is greater need for a larger number of community care facilities to establish liaison among various health centres, family practitioners and public health nurses. There is also need for provision of certain services, one of which is ascertainment services. Patients at home or in other health centres who are over 70 years of age would be visited by public health nurses and referred for any necessary examinations or services. Regular visits would be continued as a preventive measure. The value of such visits has been well demonstrated in other countries and in some areas in our country where these visits are made. Consultation services would see referrals and would provide information regarding health services and developments in geriatrics. Domiciliary visits would be made at the request of the family physician, or when the patient has no doctor, at the request of the public health nurse. This would allow the patient's social environment to be assessed, as well as his or her health.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on a little longer, but I want to give my friend, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), a chance to say a few words. I will conclude by saying it is time we looked seriously at providing alternative services which are less costly and which would enable elderly citizens to keep their rightful place in the general community environment which is far more pleasant to them than has been the case in institutions up to now.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT

speechtext:
There are a few points I want to make about Bill C-35, and I am pleased that the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) is in the House. I wish the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) were also with us, because the bill has very serious implications for immigrants to Canada. The long-term effects of the bill will be felt more by immigrants than any other group in our society.
I do not want to go over ground that has been covered already, but I welcome the provision that will allow Canadians to collect a partial pension. That is an improvement over the "all or nothing" rule that is presently the case. I welcome this in view of the fact that for health reasons many Canadians are forced to relocate, and if they do not return to Canada prior to becoming eligible for the old age pension at age 65 they lose any pension benefits they might have earned.
One might say it is not a contributory plan as is the Canada Pension, but as one of my colleagues has stated, it is contributory through the tax system. Everyone who has paid taxes in Canada in one form or another has contributed to the old age pension fund. Now the 1-40 rule will allow Canadians to collect at least a portion of the pension relative to the number
Old Age Security Act
of years they have been in Canada after the age of 18. I welcome that change.
I want to speak specifically about immigrants, however, and how the bill will affect them. The advantage for the immigrant community is that the bill will allow persons to receive pensions earned in the country of origin. In the case of residents from the United Kingdom, this has been well documented by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro). These immigrants will now see an escalation of their pensions. The pensions they receive today have been frozen and bear no relationship to the contribution they made or the years they worked and absolutely no relationship to the present cost of living. That aspect of Bill C-35 is very welcome and those members should be commended for mentioning these provisions at second reading. Not only that, but members have spoken time and time again, as well as corresponding with the minister, in an attempt to have pensions earned by former residents of the United Kingdom bear some resemblance to the cost of living here.
I should like to urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and any others involved to negotiate agreements with countries that have indicated a willingness to sign a formal pension arrangement with Canada. This bill will allow for such negotiations and arrangements, and I urge that they take place as quickly as possible.
There is a caveat, however, and I want to mention it to the minister. When speaking on the bill, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) indicated he was in favour of it because it would place everyone on an equal basis. I am not one to second-guess the hon. member on his knowledge of pension rights. In theory, he is correct. But, Mr. Speaker, he is not totally correct when you'consider immigrants coming to Canada and you look ahead over the next 40 years.
While passage of Bill C-35 will facilitate receipt of pension benefits earned in countries of former residents, the provision relates only to immigrants from countries with social security plans. For example, the United Kingdom, Italy, France and the United States have been mentioned as wanting a formal arrangement. What happens to immigrants from, for lack of a better word, developing countries? What happens when they come to Canada because there is no social security system in the country of origin?
In the last few years immigration has gone down from 200,000 to approximately 150,000. The figures are not entirely accurate, but if we take the most educated guess that we can of an annual immigration of 50,000 our net immigration at the present time is in the neighbourhood of 100,000 persons per year. What is happening is that an ever-increasing number of immigrants are coming from the developing world. Not only is that the case, but if you look at the applications you find an ever-increasing number from these countries. In fact, the pressure is so heavy at our immigration offices in some of these countries that applications are not even encouraged; the potential applicant is told he will not be accorded an interview for

February 9, 1977
Old Age Security Act
eight or 12 months. So the number of applications we might have were it not for the backlog cannot be assessed.
What happens to these immigrants who will become Canadians? After February 15 they will have that opportunity after three years' residence in this country. What happens to an immigrant from a developing country who is not even an elderly immigrant? Under the point system now, any immigrant having attained his thirty-fifth birthday or less is given ten points. For every year over the age of 35 they lose one point of those ten points. Let us consider an immigrant aged 35 who gets ten points. By awarding those ten points the department does not regard him or her as an elderly immigrant, if I can use that term. If this person then comes to Canada and works for 30 years until the age of 65, the normal retirement age, that person has worked in Canada for the majority of his or her adult life but will only be accorded three-quarters of a pension. Let us say, for example, that that person has contributed to society, as opposed to someone who has contributed very little either through work or through the tax system. I question whether that is a very responsible manner of looking at this matter. I admit that I do not have a better solution, but I wonder what will happen when we look at this regulation in the future.
What we must do as a partial solution-this is why I wish the Minister of Manpower and Immigration were here-is reassess the whole concept of sponsorship and nomination. Under the concept of sponsorship, in the new regulations, if the bill is passed, sponsorship will be allowed for parents and grandparents of any age. I am sure most members of the House have had people come to them saying they would like to sponsor their parents who are of such and such an age, and asking when they will get their old age pension. I think it is to the credit of immigrants and their concept of the extended family that they accept their responsibility toward elderly parents and grandparents.
The hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) in his closing remarks stated that we have transferred the care for the elderly to institutions. Surveys show very clearly that the greatest problem of the elderly is not health care, but loneliness. The fact is that the immigrant communities have had a keener awareness of their responsibility to older family members. I believe the Minister of Manpower and Immigration will have to look seriously at the whole question of sponsorship, in view of the fact that immigrants now coming to Canada at the age of 65, let us say, and normally receiving the old age pension at that age, will not be entitled to any more than one-quarter of the pension. The reason this is important is that if you look at demographic studies in Canada you will find that we have an aging population. This is of concern to many of us who have studied the statistics of Canada's population in the last few months, because with an aging population you also have an increased dependence factor.
So I suggest to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, as well as to the minister in whose name this bill stands, that we will need a well defined publicity campaign to explain not
[Mr. Epp.)
only to potential immigrants, but to people who will sponsor immigrants, what the changes will be. I would like to stress to the minister that it is of utmost importance that persons who apply to come to Canada as immigrants under the sponsored or nominated categories will have their benefits reduced if Bill C-35 passes.
In the remaining minutes before six o'clock I want to present one matter to the minister which is related directly to the old age pension, even though not specifically to the bill. I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will give me the latitude to present the case. I have already said that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and others have welcomed Bill C-35 because of the equality it gives to the pension scheme. But there is one form of pension that is not equal, other than the one I have mentioned already, and that is the matter of the spouse's allowance. I must say to the minister that spouse's allowance as it exists at present in the act is not equal and is not fair.
The minister might say that that question is not before us, but I believe that the entire pension plan and benefits to the elderly are open for discussion. Let us consider a case, because I believe that when we look at cases we understand a little better. Let us consider a husband who is older than his wife, which I believe is the case most often, and is receiving old age security as well as a partial or total guaranteed income supplement. His spouse is between the age of 60 and 65 and is therefore entitled to a spouse's allowance on the basis that she is married to a pensioner receiving a part or total guaranteed income supplement.
When the pensioner dies, not only does the surviving spouse lose the pension as well as the supplement, but she also loses the spouse's allowance. The majority of these unfortunate people between the age of 60 and 65 cannot go back to the labour market. Not only are they faced with personal loss and loss of pension; they are also faced with loss of this picayune spouse's allowance which they were "receiving. One might say that that is the regulation, that is the way the bill was passed by the House and there is no further argument. But the total unfairness is that there is a way out, and that is a common law relationship. The government, for purposes of spouses' allowance, accepts a common law relationship.
I say that is totally and absolutely wrong. We are saying to a widow, "No, you are not entitled to anything. You lose everything". But if I can be crude about it, we are also saying to her, "If you are shacked up with somebody, we will give you the spouse's allowance." That is totally wrong. If we could poll members on the government side, we would find that many of them would agree it is wrong because what it does is give official recognition to an illegal arrangement. In conclusion, I want to say to the minister again, even though it hits a sensitive nerve, that this is wrong and I for one want to see it changed. Let us be fair not only to immigrants under Bill C-35 but also to surviving spouses.
